What struck me most: an overwhelming number of people, regardless of party or no party, were deeply unhappy with AB 1955. Nearly everyone I spoke to—Democrats, independents, Republicans—felt it crossed a line by keeping parents in the dark about something as fundamental as their own child's well-being at school.

Why do so many representatives stop truly representing the people who need them most? The two opponents I ran against said they would represent the community, yet the County Board went ahead and implemented AB 1955 anyway.

I'm relieved the U.S. Supreme Court just stepped in and blocked enforcement of these restrictions—recognizing parents' fundamental rights to guide their children's upbringing, including on matters of faith, conscience, and family values. But I'm shocked it ever got this far in California. How did a policy infringing on parental rights, free speech, and conscience make it through our state government—only to be halted by the highest court in the land? We have thousands of elected officials here in California; why did it take nine justices to protect what should have been obvious?

Many of us—across the political spectrum—are exhausted by the constant message that if you don't fully align with the most progressive views on every issue, something's wrong with you. The framing is always the same: if you don't embrace my lifestyle or choices, you must hate me, fear me, or be bigoted. But the truth is simpler and more humane: you have every right to find joy and fulfillment in your family, your values, your morals, and what matters most to you. When those don't line up with someone else's, government has no business stepping in to "correct" or override them.

It's okay—healthy, even—when we don't share the exact same views on everything. Most of us naturally prioritize our families above friends, friends above acquaintances, and acquaintances above strangers. Our closest relationships grow from shared values, ethics, and priorities. That's not exclusion; it's human. Liberty means we get to honor those priorities without the state demanding we conform or else.

Government should secure and support what's already working in our communities—not dictate new values from Sacramento or force alignment on deeply personal matters. Lately, though, the state has gone the other way, telling families what they must accept rather than listening to what parents actually want for their kids.

The federal level matters enormously here. When laws at that level protect core rights—like parental authority and free expression—they create a safeguard. If those protections are eroded, it becomes harder for any family in any state to raise children according to their own beliefs, with no real escape.

I'm proud that the Republican Party still welcomes real debate and different viewpoints. We don't demand lockstep agreement on every issue. We can disagree passionately, still respect each other as people, and work together where we can.
